text:
The rain fell in sheets against the tall, gothic windows of Finch Manor, each drop a tiny hammer against the funereal silence within. Detective Miles Corbin hunched his shoulders against the chill, his trench coat already soaked through, as he stepped over the threshold. He’d seen a hundred crime scenes, but the sheer opulence of the grand foyer, now crawling with uniformed officers, always struck a dissonant chord. Upstairs, in the one room sealed off by yellow tape, lay the body of Lord Alistair Finch, a man whose wealth was matched only by the number of his enemies.

###

Sergeant Miller, a man whose weary face suggested he’d seen too many nights like this, met Corbin at the door to the study. "The butler found him an hour ago, sir," Miller murmured, gesturing towards the open door. "Single stab wound to the chest. No signs of forced entry. The weapon is... well, it's missing." Standing by the landing, wringing her hands, was the victim's young wife, Lady Beatrice Finch, a picture of porcelain grief, her sobs muffled by a silk handkerchief.

###

Corbin’s gaze drifted from the distraught widow to a man standing silhouetted against a large, rain-streaked window, observing the proceedings with an unnerving stillness. This was Julian Finch, Lord Alistair’s younger brother and business partner, a man known for his ruthless ambition and a temperament as cold as the marble floors. He hadn't shed a single tear, and when he finally turned to face the detective, his voice was clipped and devoid of emotion. "Detective," he said, his eyes scanning Corbin's damp coat with disdain, "let's get through these unfortunate formalities as quickly as possible."

###

"Formalities?" A sharp voice cut through the air from the shadows of the grand staircase. Corbin turned to see a young woman, her face pale and her eyes blazing with a fiery indignation that seemed out of place amidst the quiet sorrow. This was Clara Vance, Lord Alistair's personal archivist and, by all accounts, his most trusted confidante. "Is that all your brother's murder is to you, Julian? A mere inconvenience in your schedule?" Her accusation hung in the air, thick with a contempt that was almost palpable.

###

Julian’s lip curled into a sneer, a subtle but sharp dismissal of her outburst. "My grief, Miss Vance, is a private matter. I don't wear it like a costume for the benefit of others." The words struck Clara like a slap, her face flushing with anger, but before she could retort, an elderly man in a butler's uniform appeared at Corbin's elbow. He was stooped with age, his hands trembling slightly, yet his eyes held a lifetime of quiet dignity. This was Arthur Pembroke, the butler, who had served the Finch family for over forty years. "Detective," he rasped, his voice frail, "I can show you to the study now. The scene is as I found it."

###

Corbin followed the butler into the study, a sanctuary of leather-bound books and suffocating silence. Lord Alistair lay awkwardly on the expensive Persian rug, a testament to a life of luxury cut brutally short. His eyes, wide and vacant, stared up at the high, coffered ceiling. On the mahogany desk, a game of solitaire lay unfinished, the cards splayed out as if abandoned in a sudden panic. Corbin noted the expensive silver letter opener was conspicuously absent from its velvet-lined stand, leaving a perfect, empty impression.

###

"Did Lord Finch have any appointments this evening, Mr. Pembroke?" Corbin asked, his eyes still scanning the room for any detail out of place. The butler hesitated for a moment, his gaze flickering nervously towards the door where Julian had been standing. "He was expecting his brother, Detective," Arthur said, his voice barely a whisper. "They were scheduled to discuss the final details of the new merger. A rather... contentious topic between them."

###

Corbin’s attention was drawn to a small, overturned frame on the floor near the desk, partially hidden by a heavy velvet curtain. He knelt down, carefully picking it up with a gloved hand. It was a photograph of Julian and Alistair, years younger, standing on a yacht, their arms slung around each other's shoulders in a show of fraternal camaraderie that felt like a lifetime ago. The glass was shattered, a spiderweb of cracks emanating from the center, as if it had been thrown with considerable force.

###

Later, in the drawing room, Corbin began his interviews. He started with Julian, whose composure remained unshakeable. "Yes, we were to meet," Julian admitted coolly, examining his fingernails. "We argued. It’s no secret Alistair's sentimentality was about to cost us millions. He wanted to back out of the merger. I told him he was being a fool." Julian paused, a flicker of something unreadable in his eyes. "I left him to 'cool off.' When I returned, well... you'd already arrived." He provided an alibi, claiming to have been on a business call in the library, a claim that was, for the moment, unverifiable.

###

Next was Lady Beatrice. Her initial grief had subsided into a state of shocked numbness. "Alistair was… distracted lately," she confessed, twisting the large diamond on her finger. "He was worried about the merger, yes, but it was more than that. He and Julian had a terrible row last night. I heard shouting from the study. Alistair called Julian a vulture, said he would see the family name ruined before he let him take over." Her eyes welled with fresh tears. "Julian has always been so jealous of his brother."

###

Corbin's interview with Clara Vance yielded a different, more pointed perspective. Her loyalty to the late lord was fierce, her dislike for his brother equally so. "Julian is a parasite," she stated plainly, her hands clenched in her lap. "He bled Alistair's companies dry with his reckless gambles and then had the gall to demand more control. Alistair was finally cutting him off, not just from the merger, but from the family finances entirely. He was preparing the paperwork this very week. Julian knew. I'm certain of it."

###

The search of the manor continued into the late hours. A junior officer reported a discovery to Corbin. "We found this in the wastebasket in Julian Finch's private washroom, sir," he said, holding up an evidence bag. Inside was a damp, high-end handkerchief, monogrammed with a 'J.F.', stained with what looked suspiciously like a streak of dried blood. The apathetic brother, who claimed to have left Alistair to cool off, now had a much more tangible connection to the violence.

###

When confronted with the bloody handkerchief, Julian's icy facade finally cracked, if only for a second. A flicker of alarm crossed his features before being suppressed. "It's a nosebleed," he snapped, regaining his composure almost instantly. "I'm prone to them under stress. Surely you're not building a case on a man's poor sinuses, Detective?" The excuse was plausible, but the timing was damning, and Corbin could feel the weight of the evidence tipping squarely onto Julian Finch.

###

Corbin decided to re-interview the butler, Arthur Pembroke, hoping the old man's long service might have afforded him a unique insight. He found him in the dimly lit pantry, polishing silver with a methodical, almost frantic energy. "Mr. Pembroke," Corbin began gently, "did you witness the argument between the brothers last night?" The old butler paused, his cloth hovering over a silver tureen. "Witnessed it? I heard it, Detective. Like the whole house did. Mr. Julian has a terrible temper. He said things… unforgivable things to his own blood."

###

"What kind of things?" Corbin pressed. Arthur set the tureen down with a soft clink, his hands trembling more noticeably now. "He told Lord Alistair that he was a weak, sentimental old fool and that he would get what was coming to him. He said he wouldn't be stood in the way of any longer." The butler took a shaky breath. "Then, after Mr. Julian stormed out, I saw him pass the study door. He was holding something… something long and thin, wrapped in his handkerchief. He slipped it into his coat pocket before he went to the library."

###

The pieces were slotting together with an almost cinematic neatness. Motive: the merger and being cut off financially. Opportunity: he was in the house and admitted to arguing with the victim moments before his death. Weapon: the missing letter opener, which Pembroke's testimony now placed in his hand, concealed in the very handkerchief later found with blood on it. Julian Finch, the cold-hearted brother, was the clear and obvious culprit. Corbin felt the familiar, grim satisfaction of a case drawing to a close.

###

Corbin requested a full search of the library, the room Julian claimed as his alibi. The forensics team descended, dusting for prints and searching every nook. It was behind a row of leather-bound classics on Roman history that they found it. Tucked deep into the recess of the bookshelf, wrapped in a page torn from a ledger, was the missing silver letter opener. The tip was stained a dark, rusty brown. Julian's fate seemed all but sealed.

###

With the evidence mounting, Corbin brought Julian in for a final, formal interrogation. He laid out the photographs on the cold metal table: the bloody handkerchief, the hidden letter opener, the shattered picture frame. He repeated the testimony from Lady Beatrice, Clara Vance, and Arthur Pembroke. Julian watched, his face a mask of stone, but Corbin could see the trap closing around him, the subtle tightening of the muscles in his jaw.

###

"Your alibi is non-existent, your motive is clear, and we have a witness placing what we believe to be the murder weapon in your hand moments after your argument," Corbin stated, his voice flat and final. "Furthermore, the weapon was found hidden in the very room you claimed to be in. It's over, Mr. Finch." For the first time, Julian Finch looked not arrogant, but cornered and utterly defeated. He slumped in his chair, running a hand over his face. "You don't understand," he whispered, his voice raspy. "None of you understand."

###

Corbin leaned back, allowing the silence to stretch. He’d seen this act before – the last-ditch effort to sow confusion. "Then make me understand," he said, his tone unimpressed. Yet, something in Julian's eyes had shifted. The cold disdain was gone, replaced by a raw, desperate frustration. "Alistair... he was going to ruin everything," Julian began, not with malice, but with a strange, aching sorrow. "Not the merger. Something else. Something much, much worse."

###

"He was going to confess," Julian said, his voice cracking. "Decades ago, our father… he covered something up. A terrible accident at one of the old mills. A man died because of his negligence. Alistair found proof. He was going to go public, destroy the family name, our entire legacy, to soothe his own guilty conscience." He looked up at Corbin, his eyes pleading. "I argued with him, yes. I tried to talk sense into him. I took the letter opener because I was afraid he might... harm himself. He was in such a state."

###

Corbin felt a sliver of doubt, a dissonant note in his perfectly constructed theory. The shattered photograph. The unfinished game of solitaire. Signs of a struggle, yes, but also of a deeply troubled mind. "And the handkerchief?" Corbin asked, his voice losing its hard edge. "Alistair cut his hand on the broken glass of the photograph frame when he threw it," Julian explained. "I used my handkerchief to staunch the bleeding before I left. I hid the opener in the library because I didn't want the staff to find it and start gossiping about his state of mind. I was trying to protect him, not hurt him."

###

The story was plausible, rearranging all the existing facts into a new, coherent picture. But it didn't explain the stab wound. Corbin stood up and walked back to the window overlooking the rain-soaked gardens of Finch Manor. The butler's words echoed in his mind, "He has a terrible temper." And Clara's, "He was preparing the paperwork this very week." The paperwork. He turned back to the lead forensic investigator. "Get a warrant for Clara Vance's quarters. Specifically, look for any recently drafted documents and check her clothing for any trace evidence, no matter how small."

###

It didn't take them long. Tucked away in a locked briefcase under her bed were the documents Alistair had been preparing, not to cut off his brother, but to make Clara Vance a full partner, signing over a significant portion of his personal assets to her as a reward for her loyalty. And on the sleeve of the dark woolen dress she had worn that evening, the lab found a microscopic speck of blood that matched Lord Alistair's. Confronted, the archivist's composure shattered like glass. "He was going to give it all away!" she shrieked, her face contorted with a venomous rage. "To charities! To right some ancient wrong! Decades of my work, my devotion... He was going to throw it all away on a ghost! I deserved it, not them!"

###

Corbin looked at the confession scribbled on the pad in front of him. After Julian had left the study, taking the letter opener with him, Clara had entered to find Lord Alistair distraught. She tried to console him, to change his mind about his grand philanthropic gesture, but he was resolute. In a fit of furious, greedy desperation, seeing her life's work and expected inheritance vanish, she had grabbed a heavy, pointed brass finial from the curtain rod—a detail everyone had overlooked—and plunged it into his chest. She had counted on the brothers' very public feud to provide the perfect, unshakeable cover. In the end, it was not the cold brother's ambition, but the trusted confidante's avarice that had silenced Lord Alistair Finch forever.

The rain lashed against the stained-glass windows of Harrington Manor, each drop a tiny hammer against the funereal silence within. Detective Miles Corbin surveyed the scene, his gaze sweeping over the opulent library where Lord Alistair Harrington, a man whose wealth was matched only by his enemies, lay sprawled on an expensive Persian rug. A single, precise stab wound to the chest suggested a crime of passion, or perhaps cold, calculated revenge. His hand was clenched, not around a weapon, but around a small, ivory chess piece – a white knight.

###

Standing in the grand archway of the library was Lady Eleanor Harrington, a vision in silk and sorrow. Her face was a mask of aristocratic composure, yet a single, stray tear traced a path through her perfect makeup, a flaw in an otherwise flawless facade. "He was a difficult man, Detective," she said, her voice a low, steady whisper that seemed at odds with the tragedy. "He collected enemies like he collected rare books." Corbin noted the lack of hysterics, the chillingly pragmatic assessment of her late husband.

###

Corbin’s attention was drawn to a younger man pacing nervously in the adjacent drawing-room, his expensive suit rumpled and his tie loosened. This was Julian Croft, Lord Harrington's ambitious protégé and, until recently, his business partner. "We had a disagreement," Croft blurted out, his voice tight, before Corbin could even ask. "Alistair was planning to dissolve our partnership. He threatened to ruin me over the Kensington acquisition." He ran a hand through his hair, a gesture that failed to hide the tremor in his fingers.

###

A quiet presence materialized by the door, so silent that Corbin hadn't noticed his approach. It was Mr. Abernathy, the butler, a man who seemed as much a fixture of the manor as the ancient portraits on the walls. He was impeccably dressed, his face a roadmap of loyal service, but his eyes, dark and observant, missed nothing. "I found him, sir. Just after ten," Abernathy stated, his voice devoid of emotion. "Lord Harrington was in the middle of a game... he often played against himself to unwind." He gestured towards a small, ornate table where a chessboard sat, a solitary black king cornered on one side.

###

Corbin walked over to the chessboard, his eyes tracing the pieces on the mahogany and ivory squares. It was, as Abernathy had said, a game near its end, the black king trapped by a relentless white queen and rook. His gaze then drifted to the floor beneath the table, where a small glint of silver caught the lamplight. He stooped down, his gloved fingers plucking a cufflink from the deep-pile rug. It was intricately designed, a miniature black knight, its obsidian eye seeming to stare back at him accusingly.

###

Corbin held the cufflink up to the light, its polished surface reflecting the grim scene. He turned to the small, somber group. "Does this belong to anyone?" he asked, his voice even. Julian Croft's eyes widened almost imperceptibly, and his hand flew to his right shirt cuff. The cuff was bare, the small fabric hole a stark confirmation. "It... it must have come loose," he stammered, his earlier agitation escalating into visible panic. "We argued, yes, but I didn't... I would never..."

###

"An argument about a business deal that could ruin you," Corbin mused aloud, his eyes fixed on Croft. "You were here, you argued with the victim just before he died, and you leave a personal item at the scene of the crime." Each word was a carefully placed weight, pressing down on the young man's crumbling composure. Lady Eleanor watched the exchange with an unreadable expression, her hands clasped tightly in front of her, while Abernathy stood as still and silent as a statue.

###

A throat cleared softly from the doorway, drawing all eyes to a mousy-haired woman in a severe grey dress, clutching a leather-bound folio to her chest. "Forgive me, Detective," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "I am Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington's personal assistant. I overheard the… disagreement. Lord Harrington told Mr. Croft their meeting was over at precisely nine-thirty. He was quite firm. He said he would not be blackmailed." The final word hung in the air, a damning accusation that made Julian Croft's face turn ashen.

###

Corbin turned his attention to Beatrice Vance. She seemed timid, almost frightened to be the center of attention, yet her gaze was steady. "Blackmailed? What was Mr. Croft holding over him?" he asked. Beatrice clutched her folio tighter. "I... I'm not certain of the specifics, Detective. But Mr. Croft had discovered some… discrepancies… in the initial funding for the Harrington empire. Old secrets, I believe. Lord Harrington was furious that he would dare to use them against him."

###

"Old secrets, indeed," Julian Croft scoffed, a flicker of defiance returning to his eyes. "Alistair built his fortune on a lie, a swindle that bankrupted his first partner, a man named Thomas Croft—my father. He thought I didn't know. I confronted him with the proof tonight. He didn't threaten to ruin me; he laughed. He told me I was just as powerless as my father had been." The confession, raw and bitter, painted a powerful motive: revenge for a generational wrong.

###

"So you admit to a heated confrontation over a deep, personal grievance mere moments before he was murdered," Corbin summarized, his tone hardening. He paced the length of the Persian rug, his footsteps unnervingly loud in the tense silence. "You had motive, you were here at the time of death, and you left evidence connecting you to the scene. It's not looking good for you, Mr. Croft." He stopped and turned, his shadow falling over the terrified young man. "Where is the murder weapon?"

###

"I don't know! I didn't kill him!" Croft's voice cracked, desperation creeping in. "After he dismissed me, I went to the smoking room to pour myself a drink, to figure out what my next move was. I was there for at least half an hour, maybe more, stewing in my own failure. Anyone could have gone into the library then. Lady Eleanor, Abernathy... even her," he added, with a desperate nod towards the seemingly meek Beatrice Vance.

###

Corbin’s gaze shifted to Lady Eleanor, who had remained a pillar of icy calm throughout the interrogation. “Mrs. Harrington, where were you after Mr. Croft’s… meeting concluded?” Her chin lifted slightly. “I was in the east wing conservatory, Detective. I find the night-blooming jasmine to be a great comfort when Alistair was in one of his moods. I was there until Abernathy brought me the dreadful news.” Her alibi was pristine, delivered without a hint of hesitation.

###

Next, Corbin addressed the butler. "Mr. Abernathy, you found the body. What were your movements this evening?" The old butler’s posture remained ramrod straight. "After serving his Lordship his customary glass of port at nine o'clock, I retired to the kitchens to oversee preparations for tomorrow. I did my rounds of the ground floor at ten, ensuring all was secure. It was then that I discovered..." He trailed off, his professional mask slipping for a fraction of a second to reveal a flicker of genuine distress before it was gone.

###

"And you, Miss Vance?" Corbin asked, turning to the personal assistant who still hovered by the door. "Where were you after you overheard the argument?" She flinched, as if surprised to be addressed again. "I was in my office, sir, in the west wing. There were ledgers to be finalized. I… I often work late. I heard nothing after Mr. Croft left the library. The house is so large, the walls so thick." Her alibi, like the others, was plausible, a neat parcel of time and place.

###

Corbin returned to the body, kneeling beside Lord Harrington. The ivory knight was still clutched in his stiffening fingers. A man who plays chess against himself, Corbin thought, a man obsessed with strategy and control. He gently pried the fingers open. As the chess piece came free, he noticed something else: a small, almost invisible smudge of dark ink on the victim’s thumb, the kind one gets from handling freshly printed documents or, perhaps, a leaky fountain pen.

###

His eyes scanned the room again, looking for a source. Lord Harrington’s ornate desk was a model of tidiness, not a document in sight. There was an antique letter opener, a silver-framed photograph of his wife, and a gold-plated fountain pen resting in its holder, its nib clean. Nothing seemed out of place, nothing to suggest a struggle or any last-minute paperwork. The ink smudge was a loose thread, a detail without context, yet it snagged at the detective's mind.

###

"Mr. Croft," Corbin said, turning back to the primary suspect. "You said you confronted him with proof. What form did this proof take?" Julian hesitated, then sighed in resignation. "It was a set of photocopied ledgers and a letter from my father, detailing Alistair's betrayal. I had them in a briefcase. When he laughed at me, I... I threw the briefcase on his desk in disgust. I left it there." Corbin walked to the desk, running his gloved hand over the polished mahogany surface. There was no briefcase.

###

"The briefcase is gone," Corbin stated flatly, his gaze sweeping over the faces of the other three. "Someone took it." He looked at Lady Eleanor, whose expression remained impassive. He looked at Abernathy, whose posture was as unyielding as ever. Then he looked at Beatrice Vance, who was now clutching her own leather folio so tightly her knuckles were white. The folio suddenly seemed less a symbol of her profession and more like a shield.

###

Corbin walked slowly towards Beatrice, his footsteps echoing on the parquet floor. "Miss Vance, you said you were in your office all evening. Finalizing ledgers." His voice was soft, almost conversational. "It is curious, then, that Lord Harrington, a man known for his meticulous nature, would have an ink stain on his thumb when there is no ink to be seen on his desk. Unless, of course, he was handling documents just before he died. Documents that are no longer here."

###

Beatrice Vance began to tremble, her mousy demeanor dissolving into one of pure terror. "I... I don't know what you mean," she stammered, taking an involuntary step backward. Corbin's eyes dropped to the folio she was still hugging to her chest. "Let me see what you have there, Miss Vance," he said, his voice no longer gentle. It was a command, sharp and absolute, cutting through the tense air of the library.

###

With shaking hands, Beatrice held out the folio. Corbin took it and unfastened the clasp. Inside were not company ledgers, but the very documents Julian Croft had described, along with another set of papers: a freshly signed last will and testament. Lord Harrington's signature was still slightly damp at the bottom, and a single, smeared thumbprint marred the corner of the page. The new will disinherited his wife, dissolved his partnership with Croft, and left the entirety of the Harrington fortune and empire to one person: Beatrice Vance.

###

"He was going to leave it all to me," Beatrice whispered, the words tumbling out in a frantic rush. "He said he saw in me a loyalty and intelligence he'd never found in anyone else. Julian's blackmail attempt was the last straw. He called me into the library after Julian left, to sign the new will. He wanted a witness to his triumph over his so-called 'betters'." Her eyes darted wildly between the stunned faces of Lady Eleanor and Julian Croft.

###

"He signed it," she continued, her voice rising with a frantic edge, "and then... he laughed. He laughed the same way he laughed at Julian. He said the will was his final, perfect move. He told me I would be his puppet, that I would run his empire from beyond the grave, forever indebted and under his control, just like everyone else. He wasn't giving me a gift; he was forging a new chain." Her hand drifted to the letter opener on the desk, the one Corbin had dismissed as a simple desk accessory. "I was just another piece on his board. He thought he had me in checkmate. But even a pawn," she said, a chilling calm descending over her, "can take a king."

###

Corbin looked from the letter opener to the wound on Harrington's chest, then back to the quiet, mousy woman who had confessed to murder. The chess game on the table finally made sense. It wasn't about a black king cornered by a white queen; it was about the overlooked piece, the one nobody pays attention to until it reaches the other side of the board and gains unimaginable power. The cufflink, the argument, the financial ruin—it was all a brilliant misdirection, a sideshow orchestrated by Harrington's own arrogance. The true motive wasn't revenge for the past; it was a desperate, bloody bid for a future that was about to be stolen.

The rain hammered against the stained-glass windows of Blackwood Manor, each drop a tiny fist beating against the oppressive silence within. Detective Miles Corbin stood in the doorway of the study, his trench coat dripping onto the Persian rug. The room was a monument to wealth and power—towering bookshelves, a roaring fireplace, and the scent of old leather and expensive brandy. But all the grandeur in the world couldn't distract from the scene's grim centerpiece: the body of Mr. Alistair Finch, slumped in his high-backed chair, his face a mask of surprise, his final moments stolen as violently as the storm raged outside.

###

Huddled by the fireplace, clutching a silk robe tightly around her slender frame, was Evelyn Finch, the victim's young and beautiful wife. Her eyes, wide and seemingly tearless, were fixed on the detective, not on the body of her late husband. She shivered, though the fire cast a warm, dancing light across her pale, sculpted features. "He was fine just an hour ago, Detective," she whispered, her voice a fragile, trembling thing. "He sent me away… said he had an important call to make."

###

Corbin left her to her shivering and found Julian Thorne pacing the cavernous grand hall. Thorne, Finch’s long-time business rival, was impeccably dressed in a sharp suit that seemed impervious to the gloom of the manor. He barely glanced at the detective, his focus on a gold pocket watch he snapped shut with an impatient click. "Our meeting was for nine," he stated, his voice as cold and hard as his expression. "Alistair was about to sign over the controlling shares of Finch Enterprises. It seems he found a rather... permanent way to back out of the deal."

###

A fourth figure emerged from the shadows of the library, a stark contrast to the others. This was Beatrice, Alistair's long-serving and devoted housekeeper. Her face, a roadmap of wrinkles etched by decades of service and loyalty, was streaked with tears. In her trembling hand, she clutched a silver letter opener, its tip unnervingly sharp. "He and Mr. Thorne were arguing," she said, her voice raspy with grief. "Terrible things were said. Mr. Alistair threatened to ruin him completely."

###

Corbin's gaze swept over the desk, a landscape of organised chaos—papers stacked neatly, a half-empty glass of brandy, an overturned inkwell staining a sheaf of contracts. His eyes, however, were drawn to a glint of gold on the dark wood floor, partially hidden by the heavy velvet curtain. He knelt, careful not to disturb anything, and used the tip of his own pen to nudge the object into the light. It was a fountain pen, heavy and opulent, crafted from polished ebony and gold. Engraved on the clip in elegant script were the initials: J.T.

###

He pocketed the pen in an evidence bag and walked back into the grand hall, stopping directly in front of the pacing businessman. Without a word, Corbin held up the bag. Thorne’s eyes flickered towards the object for a fraction of a second, a brief flash of something unreadable in their depths before his mask of cool indifference settled back into place. "It is," he admitted coolly. "A gift. I use it for signing important documents. I must have dropped it when Alistair became... animated." A convenient explanation that did little to ease the detective's growing suspicion.

###

Corbin turned his attention back to the housekeeper, who was now straightening a slightly askew portrait on the wall, her hands fussing with the frame. "Beatrice," he said, his voice softer now. "You mentioned the argument. Tell me more. What was the tone?" She wrung her hands in her apron. "It was dreadful, sir. Not just business. Mr. Finch accused Mr. Thorne of having... improper affections for Mrs. Finch. He shouted it, for the whole house to hear. Said he'd see Thorne ruined in business and in life."

###

The detective's gaze shifted to Evelyn, who had been observing the exchange with a feigned impassivity that didn't quite reach her wide, haunted eyes. He crossed the room and stood before her, the firelight casting flickering shadows across his face. "Mrs. Finch," he asked, his tone neutral, "Beatrice says your husband accused Mr. Thorne of having feelings for you. Is there any truth to that?" A faint blush crept up her neck, a stark contrast to her pale skin. "Alistair was... a jealous man," she replied, her voice barely a whisper as she stared into the flames. "He saw threats and rivals in every shadow. Julian has always been a perfect gentleman to me."

###

Corbin nodded slowly, his mind a whirring engine of motives and opportunities. Thorne had the motive—a business deal soured by a personal accusation. He had the opportunity, being present at the manor for their meeting. And he had, apparently, left his personalized fountain pen at the scene of the crime. It was almost too neat, a perfect package tied with a bow of circumstantial evidence. Yet, the detective had learned long ago that the neatest packages were often the most deceptive.

###

He decided to press Thorne further, finding the man now staring out a rain-lashed window, his reflection a ghostly twin in the dark glass. "A jealous man, Mr. Thorne. That's what Mrs. Finch claims. But jealousy often has a spark of truth, doesn't it?" Thorne turned, his lips curled into a disdainful sneer. "Detective, my only desire was for Alistair's company, not his wife. The man was a paranoid fool whose ego couldn't fathom a deal that didn't leave him as the victor. His accusations were the desperate flailings of a drowning man."

###

Leaving the suspects to stew in the tense atmosphere, Corbin returned to the study, this time focusing on the minutiae of the room. He ran a gloved finger along the edge of the heavy mahogany desk. No signs of a struggle. The brandy glass was half-full, suggesting Finch had been relaxed, or at least not anticipating an immediate physical threat. The fatal wound, a small, precise puncture mark at the base of the skull, was barely visible amidst Finch's thick grey hair. It was a professional, almost intimate, act of violence.

###

His attention drifted back to the overturned inkwell. The dark stain spread across a series of contracts, rendering them illegible. It seemed a product of the victim's final, spasming moments. Yet, something about the shape of the spill felt wrong. It was too contained, too deliberate. Corbin crouched low, examining the spill from a different angle. Underneath the blot, just at the edge where the ink had thinned, he could make out a faint, spidery signature. It wasn't Alistair Finch's bold scrawl, but the elegant, practiced loop of Julian Thorne.

###

This new piece of evidence was damning. Thorne had claimed Finch was about to sign, but this signature suggested the deal was already done before the murder. If that was true, Thorne's primary motive—forcing the signature—evaporated. So why kill him? Was it the accusation about Evelyn? An act of pure rage? Or was the signature a forgery, meant to be obscured by the ink, a clue planted by someone else entirely to frame the obvious suspect?

###

Corbin sought out Beatrice again, finding her in the kitchen, methodically polishing silver that was already gleaming. "Beatrice, you handed me the letter opener when I arrived. Where did you find it?" he asked gently. She jumped, startled, her knuckles white around a silver fork. "It was... on the floor, sir. Near the desk. I-I picked it up without thinking. It's from his collection, you see. He treasured them. I couldn't bear to see it just lying there." Her explanation was flustered, her eyes darting away from his.

###

The detective examined the letter opener more closely. It was sterling silver, elegant and slender, with a point sharp enough to be lethal. There was no visible blood on the blade, but a professional cleaner could manage that. He made a mental note to have it tested for trace evidence. Still, Beatrice's story of simply tidying up seemed thin. Why hand it to him, drawing attention to a potential murder weapon, if she had nothing to hide? Was it a calculated act of an innocent, or the panicked misstep of a guilty party?

###

He decided to confront his prime suspect head-on. He found Thorne in the grand hall, now seated in a wingback chair, the picture of strained patience. Corbin presented him with the new evidence. "The contracts, Mr. Thorne. They were signed. By you. Before Mr. Finch's death. The spilled ink was a poor attempt to hide it. So, your story about him refusing to sign was a lie. Why?"

###

For the first time, a crack appeared in Thorne's icy composure. A muscle twitched in his jaw. "Very well, Detective. You're more perceptive than you look. Alistair signed. He conceded. But his pride couldn't handle it. He flew into a rage, spouting those vile accusations about Evelyn. He threatened to call his lawyers, to claim coercion, to drag my name through the mud for sport. I left him then, fuming in his chair. That is the truth." The story was plausible, shifting the timeline but keeping Thorne's innocence intact, conveniently placing him out of the room at the moment of death.

###

Corbin's mind raced, re-evaluating the sequence of events. Thorne's new timeline painted him as a victim of Finch's temper, not a perpetrator of violence. It also supplied a fresh motive for someone else. If Finch was about to ruin Thorne with public accusations, who would want to prevent that? Who would benefit from silencing Alistair Finch after the deal was already signed and sealed? The detective's gaze involuntarily drifted towards the fireplace, where Evelyn Finch sat, a silent, porcelain doll in the heart of the storm.

###

He approached her slowly, the crackle of the fire filling the silence between his footsteps. "Mrs. Finch," he began, his voice low and even. "Alistair signed the papers. The deal was done. But then he threatened to publicly ruin Mr. Thorne over his supposed affections for you. That would have been... unpleasant for everyone involved, wouldn't it? A messy, public scandal." Evelyn looked up, her blue eyes shimmering with unshed tears. "Alistair was a cruel man, Detective. He enjoyed hurting people. Especially those he claimed to love."

###

Corbin pressed on, the pieces clicking into a new, more sinister configuration. "He enjoyed hurting people," he repeated softly. "Did he hurt you, Mrs. Finch?" She flinched, a barely perceptible tremor that she quickly suppressed. She drew her silk robe tighter, a futile gesture of defence. "My marriage was... complicated," she evaded, her gaze dropping back to the mesmerizing flames. The confession hung unspoken in the air between them, thick with implications. A history of abuse would provide a powerful motive, one that eclipsed business deals and petty jealousies entirely.

###

"Let's reconsider the scene," Corbin said, thinking aloud as he paced before the three silent suspects. "The weapon was small, precise. It required getting close, very close, without alerting the victim. A raging business rival might have used his fists, or a heavy object. But this..." He paused, his eyes landing on the housekeeper. "This was quiet. It was personal. Executed by someone who could approach Alistair Finch without raising a single alarm." He looked from Evelyn's delicate frame to Beatrice's stooped shoulders.

###

He walked back into the study one last time, the others watching his every move. He ignored the body, the desk, the contracts. Instead, he walked over to the brandy decanter on a small side table. He lifted it to the light. It was a heavy, crystal piece, and it was nearly full. He then picked up the half-empty glass from the desk. He swirled the amber liquid, noting the aroma. It was Alistair's favourite, a 25-year-old single malt. A drink for a quiet evening. A drink one might have poured for them by a trusted hand.

###

Corbin turned to face the three figures assembled in the doorway. "Mr. Thorne, you were a distraction. Your pen, your arguments, your signature on the contract—they were all meant to draw my eye, and they did. Mrs. Finch, your husband's cruelty gave you a powerful motive, one strong enough to kill. But the act itself, the quiet intimacy of it... that belongs to someone who could walk up behind Alistair Finch's chair, unnoticed and unchallenged, while he enjoyed his evening brandy."

###

His gaze settled firmly on the housekeeper, whose face had crumpled into a mask of despair. "It was you, Beatrice," Corbin said, his voice resonating with finality. "You brought him his drink. You heard the argument with Mr. Thorne. You heard him threaten to ruin not only Mr. Thorne but Mrs. Finch as well, a woman you've watched over since she first arrived here. You couldn't bear to see him destroy another life. So you picked up one of his treasured letter openers from the desk, and while his back was turned, you ended it."

###

Beatrice didn't deny it. The tears she had been holding back finally streamed down her wrinkled cheeks, a torrent of grief and confession. "He was a monster," she choked out, her voice raw with decades of repressed pain. "He tormented his first wife to an early grave. I saw what he was doing to Evelyn... turning her into a ghost, just like her. When he signed that company away, I thought she might finally be free. But then he started shouting about ruining them... I knew he would never stop. I couldn't let him hurt anyone else." She looked past the detective, her eyes filled with a fierce, sorrowful loyalty, directly at Evelyn Finch. The rain finally stopped, leaving behind only the profound, damning silence of the truth.

The rain fell in relentless sheets against the stained-glass windows of Harrington Manor, each drop seeming to hammer a nail into the coffin of the evening. Inside the cavernous library, Detective Miles Corbin surveyed the scene with a practiced, weary eye. Lord Alistair Harrington, a man whose wealth was matched only by his list of enemies, was slumped in his favorite wingback chair, an untouched glass of amber liquid on the table beside him. There were no visible wounds, no signs of a struggle; to the casual observer, the old man could have simply drifted off into his final sleep, a peaceful end he had done little in life to deserve.

###

Standing by the grand fireplace, a nervous young man twisted a signet ring on his finger. This was Arthur Harrington, the deceased's nephew and sole heir, a man who seemed to wear his anxiety like a poorly fitted suit. "I came in to say goodnight, Detective," he stammered, his eyes darting from Corbin to the still figure in the chair. "He was just... sitting there. He hadn't even touched his nightly whiskey. I thought he was sleeping, but he was cold."

###

A figure appeared in the doorway, framed by the dim hall light, her silhouette sharp and elegant. Clad in a silk dressing gown the color of blood, Eleanor Harrington, Lord Alistair's wife of five years and thirty years his junior, surveyed the room. Her gaze, however, was as cold and hard as the marble mantelpiece; there were no tears, only a flicker of something unreadable before it was replaced by a mask of detached curiosity. "So, the old dragon finally breathed his last," she stated, her voice a low, smooth melody that held no trace of grief.

###

Corbin's gaze shifted to the untouched drink. "Did he always have a nightcap?" he asked, his voice low and even. Before Arthur or Eleanor could answer, a fourth voice, crisp and formal, answered from the hallway. Jennings, the butler, stood there, his posture as starched as his collar, his face a mask of professional solemnity. "Every evening at precisely nine o'clock, Detective. I poured it for him myself not thirty minutes before Mr. Arthur found him." His eyes flickered towards Eleanor for a fraction of a second, a silent, almost imperceptible exchange that Corbin duly noted.

###

Corbin moved closer to the wingback chair, his polished shoes silent on the thick Persian rug. He crouched beside the body, ignoring the three pairs of eyes fixed on his back. Leaning in, he detected a faint, unfamiliar scent clinging to the lapel of Lord Harrington's velvet smoking jacket. It was not the usual masculine blend of pipe tobacco and old leather, but something delicate and floral. His gaze lifted from the deceased and drifted across the room, settling on Eleanor. The cloying sweetness of gardenia seemed to emanate from her very presence, a fragrant ghost lingering in the air.

###

"Lady Harrington," Corbin began, his tone deceptively casual as he rose to his full height, "your perfume is quite distinctive. Gardenia, is it not?" Eleanor met his gaze without flinching, a small, almost mocking smile playing on her lips. "It is. A custom blend. Alistair claimed he adored it, though I suspect he merely tolerated it to keep the peace. Fragrances gave him terrible headaches." She gestured vaguely towards the decanter on the sideboard. "Hence his nightly dose of whiskey – his 'medicine,' as he called it."

###

Corbin’s eyes narrowed slightly at her casual dismissal. He turned his attention back to the immediate vicinity of the chair, his gaze sweeping the floor with meticulous care. A faint glint of light from beneath the heavy velvet ottoman caught his eye. He crouched, pulling a small evidence envelope from his coat pocket, and carefully nudged the object into view with the tip of a pen. It was a pearl earring, its silver clasp broken. Arthur gasped, his face paling further. "That's Eleanor's. I recognize it. A gift from Uncle Alistair."

###

All eyes swung to Eleanor. Her painted red lips tightened into a thin line, but her composure remained unshaken. She glided forward, peering down at the small piece of jewelry with an air of mild annoyance. "Yes, that's mine. Or rather, it was," she said, her voice dripping with disdain. "Alistair and I had a... disagreement earlier this evening. He had a tendency to grab when he was trying to make a point. He tore it from my ear. I was so furious I didn't even bother to look for it."

###

"A disagreement?" Corbin prompted, his voice a silken thread of inquiry. Eleanor sighed, a theatrical display of exasperation. "The same old argument, Detective. Money. He accused me of being a spendthrift, of draining his coffers for my 'frivolous' pursuits. He threatened to cut me off, to amend his will in favor of his precious nephew." She shot a venomous glance at Arthur, who flinched as if struck. "It was nothing new. Empty threats from a bitter old man who knew his power was slipping away."

###

Corbin let the silence hang in the air for a moment before turning to the butler. "Jennings, you said you prepared the drink. Did you see Lady Harrington near this room after her argument with her husband?" The butler’s gaze was steady, his expression impassive. "I did not, sir. After delivering the whiskey, I retired to the kitchens to oversee the preparations for tomorrow's breakfast. I heard nothing more until Mr. Arthur's cry for help." His answer was too quick, too polished, as if rehearsed.

###

"And you, Mr. Harrington?" Corbin pivoted to face the jittery nephew. "Where were you during this supposed argument?" Arthur swallowed hard, his Adam's apple bobbing. "I was in my own rooms, in the east wing. I... I could hear their raised voices, even from there. It was quite a nasty row. I didn't want to get involved, so I stayed put until things quieted down. That was about... forty minutes ago, I'd say. I waited a bit before coming down to check on Uncle Alistair."

###

Corbin paced slowly before the fireplace, his mind weaving together the threads of the evening. An argument over money, a threat to change the will, an earring torn from a lobe in anger. Eleanor had the motive and, it seemed, the opportunity. She was in the room, her scent lingering on the victim, her jewelry discarded in a struggle. Her cold demeanor did her no favors, painting the picture of a ruthless gold-digger who had finally cashed in her most valuable asset. The pieces were fitting together with an almost suspicious neatness.

###

The medical examiner arrived, a bustling, no-nonsense woman named Dr. Evans. After a brief but thorough examination, she confirmed Corbin's initial assessment. "No obvious cause of death. No marks, no contusions, save for a slight scratch on his hand. Given the circumstances and his history of heart trouble, it could be a simple coronary. But..." she paused, her brow furrowing, "I'll know for sure once I get him back to the lab. Something feels off. We'll run a full toxicology screen."

###

Corbin seized on her words. "A scratch on his hand?" He moved back to the body, Dr. Evans pointing to a small, angry red line across the back of Lord Harrington's right hand. It looked fresh. "Could have happened during the argument," Corbin mused aloud, his gaze flicking to Eleanor's perfectly manicured nails. "A wife fighting back, perhaps?" Eleanor simply raised a single, elegant eyebrow in response, offering no denial.

###

Hours later, with the body removed and the manor staff questioned, Corbin found himself back in the library. The room felt emptier now, colder. He walked over to the drinks trolley where the decanter of whiskey stood. Beside it was a small, ornate box, its lid slightly ajar. He opened it. Inside, nestled on a bed of velvet, was a collection of sugar cubes. Nothing unusual, except for one small detail. On the very top, one of the cubes had a tiny, almost invisible speck of greenish-brown powder clinging to its crystalline surface.

###

His thoughts immediately turned to poison. A substance introduced into the nightly whiskey. He carefully bagged the sugar cube, his mind racing. Who had access to this room, to the drinks trolley? All three of them, of course. Yet his mind kept circling back to Eleanor. Her argument with Alistair provided the classic motive. A scorned wife, about to be disinherited, decides to take matters into her own hands. A quiet poison, slipped into his drink, would look just like the heart attack everyone expected the old man to have eventually.

###

The following morning, Corbin received a preliminary report from Dr. Evans. "You were right to be suspicious, Miles," her voice crackled over the phone. "His blood is full of digitalis. An extract from the foxglove plant. A high enough dose would induce cardiac arrest, mimicking a heart attack almost perfectly." Corbin felt a grim satisfaction. "And the scratch on his hand?" he asked. "Defensive wound," she confirmed. "The skin under his own fingernails has traces of someone else's DNA. Also, traces of a fragrant hand cream. Gardenia, to be exact."

###

The pieces clicked into place with a definitive snap. The gardenia scent on the body, the earring, the argument, the financial motive, and now, the gardenia-scented hand cream under the victim's fingernails from a defensive scratch. Eleanor Harrington was the clear culprit. Corbin called for a uniformed officer to meet him at the manor. He would have the pleasure of seeing that cool, arrogant mask of hers finally crack. He was confident, certain. The case was all but closed.

###

Corbin arrived back at Harrington Manor, the early morning sun doing little to dispel the gloom that clung to the old house. He found Eleanor in the conservatory, calmly sipping tea and reading a book as if nothing had happened. "Lady Harrington," he announced, his voice ringing with authority, "I'm placing you under arrest for the murder of your husband, Lord Alistair Harrington." He laid out the evidence: the poison, the motive, the earring, and the final, damning clue of the gardenia-scented cream found under Alistair's fingernails.

###

For the first time, Eleanor's composure faltered. A look of genuine shock, not of fear or guilt, flashed across her face. "Gardenia hand cream?" she repeated, her voice incredulous. "Detective, you are mistaken. I can't stand the stuff. My perfume is one thing, but I would never use a cream in that scent. It's far too overpowering. The only person in this house who uses gardenia-scented hand cream is Arthur."

###

The detective froze, Eleanor's words hanging in the air like a discordant note. He replayed the evening in his mind, every detail, every glance. He had been so focused on Eleanor, on the obvious trail she left. The perfume. The earring. He had seen Arthur as weak, nervous, a pawn in the drama. But now, he remembered the young man's hands, constantly fidgeting, twisting that ring. He remembered the faint scent of flowers he'd initially attributed to Eleanor's overpowering perfume. And he remembered the butler's flicker of a glance—not at Eleanor, but towards the hallway where Arthur had been standing.

###

"Jennings," Corbin's voice was sharp, cutting through the sudden tension in the room as he summoned the butler, who appeared as if by magic. "Lord Harrington's nightcap. You said you poured it. Who was with you?" Jennings's professional facade finally crumbled, his shoulders slumping in defeat. "Mr. Arthur, sir. He came into the pantry as I was preparing the tray. Said he wanted to take it to his uncle himself, as a... a peace offering after the terrible row with Lady Harrington. He offered to add the sugar cube, as his uncle preferred."

###

Suddenly, Arthur’s anxiety made perfect sense. It wasn’t the nervousness of an innocent bystander; it was the frantic energy of a killer watching his carefully constructed plan fall apart. He had used Eleanor’s very public and very loud argument with Alistair as the perfect cover. He had counted on everyone suspecting the volatile young wife. He likely planted the earring he'd found after their fight, a piece of manufactured evidence to seal her fate. The perfume that clung to Alistair wasn't from a close embrace, but from Arthur himself, who had been doused in his aunt's signature scent after she stormed past him in the hall following the argument.

###

Corbin confronted Arthur in the library, the scene of the crime. The young man's composure shattered under the weight of the new accusations. He confessed it all, his words tumbling out in a torrent of resentment and greed. His uncle had been planning to write him out of the will after all, not because of Eleanor, but because of Arthur's mounting gambling debts. The "peace offering" was a poisoned sugar cube, laced with a digitalis concoction he'd cultivated from the foxgloves in the manor's own garden. When Alistair had realized something was wrong, that the whiskey tasted bitter, he had reached out, scratching Arthur's hand—the hand covered in the incriminating gardenia cream—in a last, desperate act.

###

As the uniformed officers led a sobbing Arthur Harrington away, Corbin stood by the window, watching the rain begin to fall once more. Eleanor stood in the doorway, her silk robe now looking less like a symbol of cold indifference and more like armor. "He used my histrionics to his advantage," she said quietly, her voice devoid of its earlier mockery. "He knew everyone would see the greedy young wife, not the desperate nephew." Corbin nodded, the misleading clues—the scent, the earring, the argument—now rearranged in his mind, forming a picture that was not only different, but terrifyingly clear. The most obvious suspect had been nothing more than a perfectly crafted distraction.

The rain lashed against the leaded glass windows of Harrington Manor, each gust of wind a mournful howl that seemed to echo through the cavernous library. Inside, the only sound was the crackle of the hearth and the quiet, steady ticking of the grandfather clock in the hall. It was this unnerving silence that Arthur Penwright, the family’s butler of thirty years, found most disturbing. He pushed open the heavy oak door to find his employer, Lord Alistair Harrington, slumped in his high-backed leather chair, a silver letter opener protruding from the starched white of his shirt. A half-empty glass of amber liquid lay shattered on the Persian rug, its contents mingling with a growing crimson stain.

###

Detective Inspector Davies arrived less than an hour later, his trench coat dripping onto the pristine marble of the foyer. A man whose weary eyes had seen too many such scenes, he surveyed the library with a practiced calm that contrasted sharply with the butler's trembling hands. Davies knelt beside the body, careful not to disturb anything, his gaze lingering not on the wound, but on a small, muddy scuff mark near the leg of the mahogany desk, a detail oddly out of place in the meticulously kept room.

###

In the drawing room, Davies found the rest of the household gathered in a tense tableau. Lady Eleanor Harrington sat bolt upright in a wingback chair, her face a mask of porcelain grief, her hands clasped so tightly in her lap that her knuckles were white. Pacing before the unlit fireplace was Julian Croft, Lord Harrington’s fiery-tempered nephew, his handsome face contorted with an emotion that looked more like fury than sorrow. Observing them both from a distance was Dr. Alistair Finch, the family physician, a quiet, unassuming man whose presence seemed almost an afterthought.

###

"My condolences, Lady Harrington," Davies began, his voice a soft rumble. "Can you tell me when you last saw your husband alive?" Eleanor's gaze was distant, fixed on a point beyond the rain-streaked window. "He retired to the library after dinner, as was his custom. He said he had some papers to review." She paused, dabbing a lace handkerchief at the corner of her eye, a gesture that seemed more practiced than heartfelt. "I heard shouting a short while later. It was Julian. He was demanding money again, and Alistair… Alistair was finally refusing him. He threatened to write him out of the will entirely."

###

Davies turned his gaze, which had all the warmth of a winter sea, to the pacing nephew. "Mr. Croft. Your aunt mentioned an argument concerning money and the will." Julian scoffed, running a hand through his disheveled hair. "Of course we argued! He was a cantankerous old goat who delighted in holding his fortune over my head. I told him he couldn't control me forever." He stopped abruptly, his jaw tight. "But I didn't kill him. I may have been furious, but I'm not a murderer. I just… needed to get some air."

###

"And you, Doctor?" Davies's attention shifted to the quiet physician. "What brought you to the manor on such a foul evening?" Dr. Finch adjusted his spectacles, his expression unreadable. "Lord Harrington summoned me. He'd been complaining of some chest pains earlier. I was waiting in the hall for him to conclude his business with his nephew." He gestured vaguely in Julian's direction. "The shouting was... quite pronounced. I thought it best not to intrude." Davies’s eyes flicked down, noting the doctor’s impeccably clean shoes before they settled on Julian's. The younger man’s brogues were indeed damp, with small, tell-tale specks of mud clinging to the welts, a perfect match for the mark in the library.

###

Inspector Davies turned back to the butler, who had been standing silently by the doorway, a ghost in his own home. "Mr. Penwright, you discovered the body. Tell me precisely what you observed after the argument." The butler swallowed, his Adam's apple bobbing. "I heard the shouting cease, sir, followed by the library door slamming shut. A moment later, I saw Mr. Croft storming down the west wing corridor. He looked… well, he looked enraged. He didn’t seem to see me at all as he went straight out the side door into the garden. It was perhaps five minutes later that I entered the library to check on his Lordship."

###

Davies's eyes narrowed on Julian Croft, who had stopped his pacing and was now watching the interrogation with a defiant sneer. "You went out into the garden, you said? In this downpour?" Davies's voice was deceptively mild. "It seems a rather odd time for a constitutional. You stormed out of the library, slammed the door, and went straight outside, just moments before your uncle was found dead. It paints a rather incriminating picture, wouldn't you agree, Mr. Croft?" The accusation hung in the air, thick and heavy as the scent of wet wool and old books.

###

A bitter laugh escaped Julian’s lips, a sound utterly devoid of mirth. "Oh, this is rich. Yes, I was angry. Yes, I went outside to keep from putting my fist through a priceless Ming vase. And yes, my shoes are muddy. It’s a garden, Inspector, it tends to get muddy in a bloody downpour." He took a half-step towards the detective, his voice dropping to a low, challenging growl. "You think I’d be stupid enough to stab the old man and then traipse mud all over the crime scene? I wanted his money, not his life. A dead man can't sign a cheque, Inspector."

###

Unfazed by the outburst, Davies redirected his attention to Lady Eleanor, whose composure remained impeccable, almost unnaturally so. "Lady Harrington, your husband's business… was it going well? Were there any recent pressures or concerns that he mentioned to you?" She delicately smoothed a non-existent wrinkle in her silk dress. "Alistair was always meticulous. The Harrington shipping line is a legacy, Inspector. It is… was… an empire. Of course, there are always rivals, but he never spoke of any specific threats. He kept his business affairs very private." Her words were precise, yet revealed nothing, like a beautifully crafted but empty porcelain vase.

###

Davies excused himself and returned to the silence of the library, the scent of leather and old paper now tainted with something metallic and grim. He circled the large mahogany desk, his eyes scanning the surface. Amidst a neat stack of shipping ledgers was a single sheet of foolscap, penned in Lord Harrington’s precise, spidery script. It was a hastily drafted codicil to his will, the ink barely dry. With a gloved hand, Davies read the damning words: "…and to my nephew, Julian Croft, for his continued insolence and profligate nature, I hereby bequeath nothing, revoking all previous entitlements." The document was dated that very evening.

###

Returning to the drawing room, Davies held the codicil aloft. "Mr. Croft, I believe this is what your argument was truly about." He read the lines aloud, his voice flat and devoid of emotion. "Your uncle was in the process of disinheriting you completely. You saw this, didn't you? You knew that once he signed it, your life of leisure was over. A powerful motive for a man of your... temper." The color drained from Julian's face, his earlier bravado crumbling into a shocked, ashen disbelief. He stared at the paper as if it were a venomous snake.

###

"He… he wouldn't," Julian stammered, shaking his head. "He always threatened, but he never would have gone through with it. It was a game to him, a way to keep me under his thumb." He looked around the room, his eyes wild and pleading, but found no sympathy. The rain fell in sheets against the leaded glass of Blackwood Manor’s grand study, a relentless drumming that seemed to count out the final, silent seconds of Alistair Blackwood's life. Inside, the old magnate was oblivious to the storm. He lay sprawled behind his mahogany desk, a single, dark stain blooming on the pristine white of his shirt, a heavy silver letter opener lying inches from his outstretched hand. The scream that tore through the oppressive silence belonged to Eleanor, his young wife, who stood framed in the doorway, her face a mask of porcelain horror.

###

Her cry was answered by thundering footsteps from the adjoining billiards room. Arthur Vance, Alistair’s long-suffering business partner, burst in, his face ashen and his usually immaculate tie slightly askew. He stopped short, his eyes wide, taking in the scene with a choked gasp. Moments later, Beatrice Blackwood, Alistair's stern, older sister, appeared at the top of the grand staircase, her descent slow and deliberate. Her gaze, cold as the marble floor, swept over the scene before settling not on her brother’s body, but on Arthur’s panicked face.

###

It was less than half an hour before Detective Inspector Corbin arrived, his trench coat dripping onto the pristine oriental rug. He was a weary but sharp-eyed man, admitted by a stoic butler, Jennings, whose loyalty to the Blackwood name seemed as old and cracked as the manor’s foundations. Corbin took in the scene with a practiced glance: the weeping widow, the pacing business partner, the statuesque sister. "Nobody leaves this house," he stated, his voice calm but carrying an undeniable authority. "I'll need to speak with each of you individually."

###

Corbin began his examination of the study, his movements methodical and quiet. He knelt beside Alistair’s body, noting the position of the letter opener and the lack of any obvious signs of a struggle on the desk itself. His gaze swept the room, cataloguing the expensive books, the decanters of amber liquid, the cold hearth. Then, his eyes caught a glint of gold near the heavy velvet drapes that concealed the rain-lashed French doors. Using his pen, he carefully nudged a small, circular object from beneath the fabric: a cufflink, engraved with the ornate, unmistakable initials 'A.V.'

###

With a delicate maneuver, Corbin dropped the cufflink into a small evidence bag, his face an impassive mask. His attention then shifted to the French doors themselves. He ran a gloved finger along the brass handle, noting that the bolt was not thrown—a detail that suggested either a hurried exit or an expected arrival. From across the room, he saw Arthur Vance stiffen, the man's gaze darting from the detective's actions near the window to his own wrist, where a matching cufflink gleamed under the lamplight. A single bead of sweat traced a path down Arthur’s temple.

###

"Mr. Vance, if you would," Corbin said, his voice cutting through the tense silence. He gestured towards the library across the hall, its leather-bound books casting long shadows in the dim light. Arthur swallowed hard, his Adam's apple bobbing, and followed the detective, his posture stiff and defensive. "You and Mr. Blackwood had a disagreement recently, I'm told," Corbin began, foregoing any pleasantries as he leaned against a heavy oak desk. Arthur flinched, his eyes wide. "That's a gross oversimplification," he stammered. "We had a... a difference of professional opinion regarding the new merger. Alistair was being reckless, risking everything we'd built!" His voice rose with agitation, betraying a depth of frustration that felt far more personal than professional.

###

Corbin remained silent for a moment, letting Arthur’s agitated words fill the space between them. "And this merger," the detective continued, his tone deceptively casual, "would it have benefited you financially if Alistair had... backed out? Or was removed from the equation entirely?" Arthur paled, the accusation hanging unspoken in the air. "It would have ruined me!" he retorted, his voice cracking. "Alistair held the majority shares. His refusal to sign meant the deal would collapse, taking my entire personal fortune with it. I was trying to save us, not destroy him!"

###

Leaving a shaken Arthur Vance in the library, Corbin sought out Eleanor, the young widow. He found her in the drawing-room, huddled in a large armchair, clutching a silk handkerchief. Her sobs had subsided into quiet, shuddering breaths. "Mrs. Blackwood," Corbin began gently, "I know this is difficult, but can you tell me what you saw?" Eleanor looked up, her blue eyes swimming with tears. "I... I was coming to bring Alistair his evening tea. He always took it at nine. The door was ajar, and I saw... I saw him," she choked out, a fresh wave of grief washing over her. "Before that," Corbin pressed, "did you hear anything? Voices? An argument?" She shook her head. "No, just... just Arthur. He was with Alistair earlier, in the study. Their voices were raised. It sounded terrible."

###

Corbin thanked the grieving widow and made his way to Beatrice Blackwood's private sitting room. She sat bolt upright in a high-backed chair, her hands folded primly in her lap, showing none of the emotional turmoil of the others. "My brother was a fool in business and a fool in love," she stated without preamble, her voice as brittle as dry leaves. "He trusted Arthur, a man whose ambition has always outstripped his talent. And he married that... that girl, who was clearly only after his money." Her eyes narrowed. "I warned him about Arthur just this afternoon. I told him I'd seen the man tampering with the safe in the study last week. Alistair just laughed it off."

###

The mention of the safe piqued Corbin's interest. He returned to the study, the scene now illuminated by the harsh glare of a portable police lamp. He located the safe, cleverly concealed behind a large oil painting of a grim-faced ancestor. Running a gloved finger along the dial, he found it cold and undisturbed, but noted several deep scratches near the combination dial, fresh gouges in the dark metal that seemed to corroborate Beatrice's claim of tampering. It was a lock that would require skill or force to open, and the marks suggested a failed, frustrated attempt.

###

Corbin then turned his attention to the desk. He meticulously sorted through the stacks of paper, most of them business documents and ledgers. Tucked beneath a blotting pad, however, he found something different. It was a single sheet of embossed letterhead from a prestigious law firm, dated just two days prior. The text was brief and formal, confirming an appointment for Alistair Blackwood to make significant alterations to his last will and testament. The appointment was for the following morning.

###

With this new piece of information, Corbin decided to press Arthur Vance again. He found the man pacing relentlessly in the billiards room, his face a mask of anxiety. "Changing his will," Arthur scoffed when Corbin presented the letter. "Of course he was. He was planning to write me out completely, all because I wouldn't support his disastrous merger. He told me as much during our argument. He said by tomorrow, I wouldn't be worth the ink on his signature." His hands clenched into tight fists at his sides, his knuckles white with fury.

###

The pieces were beginning to form a damning picture, and Arthur Vance was at its center. A man on the brink of financial ruin, facing complete disinheritance, who had argued violently with the victim just hours before his death. His cufflink was found at the scene, near a potentially unlocked escape route. Beatrice claimed he'd been trying to crack the safe, and Eleanor overheard their heated confrontation. It was a classic case of greed and desperation, almost too neat, too textbook. Yet, Corbin couldn't shake a feeling of unease, a nagging sense that one of the brushstrokes in this grim portrait was out of place.

###

Corbin decided to re-examine the murder weapon. The silver letter opener was heavy, ornate, and now stained with Alistair's blood. He carefully inspected the handle, a twisted design of ivy leaves. Within the intricate metalwork, almost completely obscured by the dark, drying blood, he spotted it: a single, long strand of blonde hair, caught tightly in a crevice of the silver. It was a detail easily missed, a pale thread against the gleaming metal.

###

Holding the evidence bag containing the hair up to the light, Corbin's mind raced. Arthur Vance's hair was dark and receding. Beatrice's was a severe, iron-grey bun. Alistair himself had been mostly bald. That left Eleanor, the beautiful, weeping, blonde widow. It was a jarring contradiction to the mountain of evidence pointing squarely at Arthur. Could she have been involved? Or was it merely a stray hair, transferred from an embrace or a shared moment earlier in the day? The simplicity of the motive against Arthur warred with the stark physical evidence in his hand.

###

Corbin requested to see Eleanor's chambers. She granted permission with a listless wave of her hand. The room was a stark contrast to the rest of the manor; modern, airy, and filled with light colors. On her vanity table, amidst an array of perfumes and silver-backed brushes, lay a small, velvet-lined jewelry box. The detective, with her permission, opened it. Inside, nestled amongst pearls and diamonds, was a collection of exquisite, antique cufflinks, a hobby she'd apparently curated for her husband. At least, that's what one would assume.

###

He returned to Eleanor in the drawing room, holding the evidence bag with the single strand of hair. "Mrs. Blackwood, this was found on the murder weapon," he said, his voice neutral. She visibly recoiled, her hand flying to her mouth. "That's... that's impossible," she whispered, her eyes wide with what looked like genuine shock and fear. "I was nowhere near... I loved my husband. Why would I...?" Her composure finally shattered, and she dissolved into heaving, desperate sobs.

###

Corbin left her to her grief, the performance, if it was one, utterly convincing. He found Jennings, the butler, polishing silver in the pantry, his movements slow and methodical. "Jennings," Corbin began, "you've been with this family a long time. Tell me about Mrs. Blackwood. The first Mrs. Blackwood." The butler paused, his polishing cloth held mid-air. "Ah, Clara," he said, a ghost of a smile touching his thin lips. "She passed ten years ago. A lovely woman. Fair-haired, like the current Mrs. Blackwood. Alistair never truly got over her. He kept all her things, just as she left them."

###

"And where are her things kept, Jennings?" Corbin asked, a new theory beginning to crystallize in his mind. The butler gestured with his head towards the upper floors. "In the old west wing, sir. Untouched for a decade. Mr. Blackwood couldn't bear to have them cleared out. He called it her 'memory room'." Corbin felt a jolt of understanding. A blonde hair didn't have to belong to a living blonde. It could be a memento, a remnant from a place steeped in the past.

###

With Jennings' key, Corbin entered the west wing, a layer of dust covering everything like a fine shroud. The 'memory room' was just as the butler described it; a suite of rooms preserved in time. A woman's dressing gown lay across a chair, and on the vanity, a silver-backed brush lay untouched. Corbin carefully examined the brush. It was filled with long, blonde hairs, identical in color and texture to the one he'd found on the letter opener. He realized the hair wasn't a clue to the killer's identity, but to the victim's state of mind.

###

He returned to the study and stood over the body, the pieces of the puzzle now rearranging themselves into a completely different picture. The letter opener lay near Alistair's hand, not gripped within it. The note about the will, the fierce argument with Arthur—it wasn't a prelude to murder, but to something else entirely. Alistair, facing financial ruin from a bad deal and haunted by the memory of his first wife, was a man in despair. Corbin now saw the scene not as a homicide, but as a meticulously staged suicide, designed to look like anything but.

###

But a staged suicide still needs a stage manager. Someone had to plant the cufflink, scratch the safe, and subtly guide the narrative. Who benefited most from Arthur Vance being framed for murder? Not Eleanor, who would simply inherit. Not Arthur himself, obviously. His eyes settled on the figure standing silently in the hall, watching him with an unnerving stillness. Beatrice Blackwood. She had despised her brother's new wife and his business partner. With Alistair dead and Arthur imprisoned, the entire Blackwood fortune, every last share and title, would revert to the only remaining blood relative: her.

###

"Miss Blackwood," Corbin called out, his voice echoing in the grand hall. Beatrice turned her head slowly, her expression unreadable. "It was a clever plan. My brother kills himself, despondent over his failing business and his dead wife, but you couldn't let it be that simple, could you?" He walked towards her, his steps deliberate. "You saw your chance to get rid of the two people you despised most. You took Arthur's cufflink from his coat when he rushed in, dropping it by the window. You invented the story about the safe to cement his motive of greed. You ensured we saw him as a desperate, violent man."

###

Beatrice’s cold composure finally cracked, a flicker of fury animating her stone-like features. "My brother was a weak fool who was squandering our family's legacy on a gold-digging harlot and a feckless partner!" she spat, her voice laced with a lifetime of resentment. "He was going to ruin us all. His suicide was a final act of cowardice, but it presented an opportunity. Arthur was the perfect scapegoat. It was a fitting end, tidying up all of my brother's loose ends in one fell swoop." She didn't confess to murder, but to manipulation, a crime of cold, calculating opportunism.

###

Corbin shook his head slowly. "You almost got away with it," he conceded. "But you misunderstood one crucial detail." He gestured back towards the study, towards the letter from the lawyer. "He wasn't changing his will to cut Arthur out. He was changing it to put him back in, to give him controlling interest. His last act wasn't to ruin Arthur, but to save him from the merger's fallout, a final apology. Alistair killed himself, yes. But your deliberate, malicious framing of an innocent man to secure your inheritance," Corbin said, pulling out a pair of handcuffs, "is a crime all its own."
